column2: Everyone knows that Saint Patrick is so well-regarded among irish christians and insulars and his feast day draws large crowds each year. Saint Patrick's Day is traditionally celebrated with a joyous procession through the streets followed by a series of raucous nighttime feasts. It is also customary to wear green clothing, the color of Saint Patrick.
I must find my green robes...

The annual Saint Patrick's Day procession has begun. Your capital's streets are filled with green-clad pilgrims from across the land, and the air is filled with the sounds of cheers and ancient ballads. Many of the pilgrims make a large show of throwing away and trampling over decorative snakes, imitating Saint Patrick's feat of driving away snakes from his native land.

Night has fallen, and the procession has come to an end. The people are now heading to local taverns for the start of the second half of the celebration — the feasts. These "feasts" usually devolve into drunken, hedonistic revelry, so more religious [Root.Religion.GetName]s frown on them. However, they are still an integral part of the celebrations for most.
I think I'll pass this year.
You get a little carried away with your drink...
Saint Patrick's Day comes to an end.

You wake up in an alleyway, with the sun shining overhead and your head pounding in pain. Your memory slowly begins to return to you. You went to a tavern last night after the Saint Patrick's Day procession. Then you went to another tavern... and another tavern... You wince in pain after glancing up at the sky. You should probably get some rest.

You wake up in an alleyway, with the sun shining overhead and your entire body aching in pain. Your memory slowly begins to return to you. Someone at the tavern started a fight with you... or perhaps you started a fight with them? In any case, the entire tavern ended up joining the melee, and now you're paying the price...
I don't think I can walk this off...

You wake up in your bed, feeling tired yet oddly happy. Your memory begins to return to you. You had a great time at the tavern! You sang many ballads, told a few somewhat embellished stories, and were generally the center of attention all night. And the best part? You don't even have a hangover!
I can't wait for next year!

You wake up in an unfamiliar bed, in an unfamiliar room... next to an unfamiliar person. As you struggle to remember what you did last night, you hear a crude-sounding, alcohol-scented voice from the other side of the bed. "Morning there, [Root.GetLadLass]. You wanna go again? I haven't had a tumble that good in ages, and that's really saying something."

Every insular is attached to sacred sites in the British Isles. Glastonbury Abbey and Glendalough, Knock and Iona, and many other sites that bear witness to events described in legend and hagiographies. Some insulars also dare to travel beyond the Isles, to Jerusalem, Nazareth, and Bethlehem, which are mentioned in the Bible. As one of the insulars, you too can embark on this journey for the glory of the Lord.

As a follower of Insular Christianity, you have undertaken a difficult pilgrimage to a holy site that your fellow believers traditionally hold in special respect and veneration. As a pilgrim planning your pilgrimage, you have many destinations to choose from. You can travel to the heart of the Insular pilgrimage movement, such as Glastonbury Abbey or Glendalough, or you can venture to less popular pilgrimage destinations. You can also undertake the extraordinary task of journeying all the way to the Holy Land, the place where Jesus Christ was born, taught, and crucified over 2,500 years ago.
Go on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land
Visit one of the most popular pilgrimage destinations

Glastonbury Abbey, the ruins of Iona, the site of Marian apparitions in Knock and Glendalough, the heart of Irish monasticism, are the most popular pilgrimage destinations among your fellow believers.

Among your coreligionists, besides the Holy Land and places like Glastonbury and Iona, also respected, though less visited, places like Westminster Abbey, Walshingham, St. Patrick's Purgatory and Kells are held in high esteem.
Everything is packed and you can set off on your pious pilgrimage.

You reach Nazareth, a city north of Bethlehem, where you are heading from Jerusalem. This is where your Lord and God, Jesus Christ, grew up and lived as a carpenter's son under the supervision of his guardian, St. Joseph, and his mother, Mary. As a pilgrim from distant islands, you are astonished by all the buildings you see and feel a great sense of awe at the entire city. You visit all the churches in this city, including the Basilica of the Annunciation, and end at St. Joseph's Church, where, according to legend, the workshop where St. Joseph worked was located. You stop there and immerse yourself in prayer, worshiping God, praising his Mother, Mary, and asking St. Joseph for intercession.
Here Christ grew up... a truly beautiful city...

column3: it was here that Solomon built the First Temple, and the Jews, after the Babylonian Captivity, built the Second. It was here that Jesus Christ taught, arriving on a donkey. Here the Last Supper took place, where Christ instituted the Holy Mass and changed the bread into his body and the wine into his blood. Here he was betrayed, crucified under Pontius Pilate, crucified, and buried. You walk through this city, amazed. Here lies the true confluence of the three greatest religions: Christianity, Judaism, and Islam. You see pilgrims of various Christian denominations, Arab and Jewish merchants. You head on and visit the successive Christian temples located here.

column2: Here Christ taught... a truly beautiful city...

You reach Bethlehem, once a small town, now a large city. It was here that Mary and Joseph stopped, and, unable to find a place to stay in a normal apartment, they stopped in a stable, where Mary gave birth to a son. It was here that shepherds and animals witnessed the birth of the Messiah, and it was here that the three wise men came from the East to give him gold, frankincense, and myrrh. And here you visit all the churches, ending at the Church of the Nativity, built, as legend has it, on the site of Christ's birth. You enter, captivated by the beauty of this place. It is here that your journey ends
column3: you have arrived at the place where the Lord was born, though for reasons beyond your control, you were "late" by over 2,500 years. You kneel before the altar and immerse yourself in silent prayer, thanking God for taking you so far from home.

column2: Here Christ was born... a truly beautiful city...

The Benedictine Order is an old monastic community with 'Ora et Labora', meaning 'pray and labor', as their motto. Often recognized by their black habits, they worship God and find purposein prayer and quiet contemplation as well as scholarly work.
